While the daellash adult is a solitary ambush predator, its young benefi t from staying near their kin. Dozens expose their heads into 
the vacillating current of the waves near the shoreline from tiny little burrows they dig their long bodies. Waiting to snatch any stray 
fi sh with their trap-like jaws and, just as quickly, retreating into the sand when something larger nears.
A single large eye peers from a shell half-buried in the sand, waves of the tide break upon the small outcropping and patiently it 
waits for the telltale slap of a flopping stranding fi sh. Bubbles pop and spew eagerly from its maw as the little mollusk spies its land-
trapped prey and, with a shimmy and tug, it pulls itself from the sand and rushes over to the glistening meal.
Small and thin shelled compared to its adult form, the baby vortautilus swims low to the ocean floor, rushing into the safety of dug 
tunnels made from older kin. Typically feasting on the remains of their hunt, the babies will rarely, if ever, engage in any combat; 
instead will use their nascent ethanol streams to keep aggressive beasts at bay.
Chittering amongst its young spawn, the energetic illithisk juveniles instinctively rub up against the larger adults, often pestering the 
larger crustaceans, and getting a sharp wack of their scythe-like arms to ward them off. While annoying, this behavior prompts the 
adult's symbiotic urchin to germinate and spread to the younger generation of crustaceans.
